paragraphs.heading: Where river meets sea
paragraphs.text: An estuary is a partly enclosed body of brackish water on the coast, where fresh water from rivers or streams mixes with salt water from the sea. It is a transition zone between river and ocean, and so counts as an ecotone, a place where different ecosystems overlap. Both sides shape it: the sea through tides, waves and salty water pushing inland, and the river through its flow of fresh water and the sediment it brings.

paragraphs.heading: Pinning down a definition
paragraphs.text: The word comes from the Latin aestuarium, a tidal inlet of the sea, itself from aestus, meaning tide. The most widely accepted definition describes a semi-enclosed coastal water body with a free link to the open sea, where sea water is measurably diluted by fresh water draining off the land. That leaves out coastal lagoons and brackish seas, so a broader definition lets the fresh water inflow stop at times, the sea link close for part of the year, and the tides have little effect. Under the broader version, fjords, lagoons, river mouths and tidal creeks all count.

paragraphs.heading: Tides, mixing and nutrients
paragraphs.text: Sea water enters an estuary with the rhythm of the tides and is diluted by water from rivers and streams. How that dilution plays out differs from one estuary to the next, depending on how much fresh water arrives, the tidal range, and how much water evaporates. The mixing also delivers plenty of nutrients, in the water and in the sediment, which makes estuaries some of the most productive natural habitats in the world.

paragraphs.heading: Nurseries and natural filters
paragraphs.text: Freshwater, marine and land species live side by side in estuaries and build complex food webs. Many marine fish and shellfish spend their early lives there, and estuaries also support mangroves, seagrasses, salt marshes and seaweeds. Migratory birds and endangered species find habitat there too. Wetlands such as swamps and salt marshes filter the sediment, nutrients and pollutants washed down from upland areas, and marsh grasses hold shorelines in place, cushioning storms and sea-level rise.

paragraphs.heading: How estuaries formed
paragraphs.text: Most estuaries today date from the Holocene, when the sea began to rise about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago and flooded valleys cut by rivers or scoured by glaciers. The commonest type in temperate climates is the drowned river valley, also called a coastal plain estuary, where rising sea water creeps up a river valley and the estuary keeps the valley's shape; Chesapeake Bay is one. Bar-built estuaries form where sediment has piled up as fast as the sea rose, leaving shallow water cut off from the ocean by sand spits or barrier islands. Fjords formed where Pleistocene glaciers deepened and widened river valleys into a U shape.

paragraphs.heading: Under pressure
paragraphs.text: Many estuaries are in decline. Causes include soil erosion, deforestation, overgrazing, overfishing and the filling-in of wetlands. Other pressures are eutrophication linked to excess nutrients from nitrogen runoff, sewage and animal waste; pollutants such as heavy metals, polychlorinated biphenyls, radionuclides and hydrocarbons from sewage; and dikes or dams built for flood control or water diversion.
